title: Argentine Rapper Dillom Unleashes ‘La Nueva Violencia’ Album: ‘I’m Part of the System & Also a Victim Who Gets Caught Up In It’
summary: With his third album, Dillom explores his relationship with the cultural system that propelled his rise to fame, while also leaving him stuck in some potentially destructive cycles.
contentText:
2021: “I don’t have dreams, I have plans. I don’t have enemies, I have fans.”

2024: “Little by little, I became my own worst enemy, searching for myself in an empty shell.”

2026: “Don’t pay anymore to watch me lie.”

Read as a sequence, these three lines could form a Buenos Aires-inspired take on F. Scott Fitzgerald’s The Great Gatsby (1925): the tragedy of the self-made man who becomes trapped by the identity he built to save himself. Post Mortem (2021) was the coronation of a 20-year-old kid who, alongside his label Bohemian Groove, crafted himself into an abrasive rock star. Today, that persona doesn’t go out hunting for victims anymore — it feeds off its creator.

La Nueva Violencia , released Wednesday (Aug. 12) under his own independent label Bohemian Groove, is self-devouring, reflected across 13 tracks and a voice memo from his father. In it, Dillom questions the ills of contemporary society — ones he can never fully prove his innocence against.

“I feel like telling the whole world to f–k off… But I’m not going to say it.” That’s how Dylan León Masa (his real name) kicked off this cover interview with Billboard Argentina . It’s been three days since the World Cup final, but the digital world is still packed with a never-ending line of people eagerly waiting their turn to rage at Argentina with a nervous kind of fury. Once again, social media has activated its punitive function, highlighting how quick people are to point out others’ flaws while avoiding any self-reflection. “I kind of nailed the timing of the album,” he notes. In the meantime, the present moment only amplifies the meaning behind its title.

The evidence points to him, even though the responsibility belongs to everyone. The system judges him, consumes him, and then demands another season. It’s been a while since he’s been “part of the common people” (as he sings in “Gente Común”), and selling out Vélez Stadium (Estadio José Amalfitani) this past Dec. 20 only solidified that distance. The spectacle promises a movie more captivating than the plot itself. Between a flawless teaser and another viral moment online, poverty, wars, and the everyday misery of life remind us that there are still parts of reality that can’t be turned into a campaign. He wrestles with desires that his conscience objects to, but when it’s time to act, he ends up dancing in the same play.

“I’m part of the system and also a victim who gets caught up in it,” he admits, as a smile slightly distorts the juice box tattoo on his left cheek. “It’s impossible not to be, because you enjoy it,” he says.

When he thinks about his biggest enemies, his own name makes the top five. The breaking point comes when Dylan, Dillom, and the identities in between lose the distance that once allowed them to view reality as something external. His intense journey through the cadence of Buenos Aires — from his hometown of Colegiales to Villa 31, where he first cut his teeth as a producer — gave him an early awareness of social diversity. This experience intertwined with a family history that the artist has openly shared in several interviews and continues to draw from in his writing, as seen in “OPA,” his first major hit. Fame, for its part, only made his contradictions more apparent.

“I’m someone who’s very at peace with my contradictions, so I can express them,” he says now, at 25. “In fact, they really fascinate me as a source of inspiration.”

Out of that unease came La Nueva Violencia (or The New Violence). “I started feeling dizzy about the present. I’d think, ‘Man, everything’s so messed up, this can’t be real.’” The constant exposure to videos of wars, drones, propaganda, and “a ton of crappy information” began to feel like a form of siege. “Technology has changed the mechanisms of persuasion. I started finding it both horrifying and super interesting at the same time,” the artist explains. However, his critique doesn’t come from a place of moral superiority over what he’s questioning. “I don’t like hypocrisy or that moral high ground people use to attack these issues.”

Andrés Capasso

Resisting every temptation to conform, Dillom once again distances himself from the commercial mechanisms of the music industry to speak about what he’s going through. For instance, none of the collaborators are listed on the tracklist — not even St. Vincent, Sebastian Murphy from Viagra Boys, Declan Mehrtens of Amyl and the Sniffers, Miranda!, Juana Aguirre, Juana Rozas, Babeblade, or Terra (there’s also a hidden collaboration no one is allowed to talk about). The album cover, designed by his visual partner Noduermo (Andrés Capasso), ties the concept together: Inside a toy house, miniature dolls and a plastic showgirl display signs of a prematurely adult world, while a tiny Dylan watches through the window, contemplating his possible destiny.

With sharp, absurd and controversial lyricism, Dillom crafted an album that highlights the vices the average household swallows between the morning news and a phone propped up on a pillow. And, of course, he doesn’t leave out his own living room: women, drugs, sex, and that rock-and-roll masculinity so often sold as rebellion. He throws in “Mercado Pete” — a sexually charged play on words referencing Mercado Pago, Argentina’s popular payment platform — takes shots at “the idiots on Gran Hermano,” and imagines a kind of Shazam to identify women as if they were songs, joking that he plans to patent it.

He can shift to romance in “Souvenir,” telling a girl they still have plans to make together, “like going to a motel in General Paz,” or puff himself up in “Cocodrilo” with a line like, “I’m the star of my own stage.” After embracing a Daft Punk-inspired creed in “ Nadie coge gratis ” (“Nobody F–ks for free”), stepping into “the bisexual bathroom,” and greeting everyone with a casual “ hola, qué tal ” (“hi, how are you”), he admits he’s starting to get used to the hangovers.

The venue chosen for the first listen was Panda, the legendary studio where iconic albums like Oktubre (1986) by Patricio Rey y sus Redonditos de Ricota and Yendo de la Cama al Living (1982) by Charly García were recorded. Unlike his previous album, Por Cesárea (2024), Dillom no longer delegates conflict to a fictional construction. Speaking to a small group of journalists, the artist quickly dismissed any notion of a cohesive narrative: this wasn’t a conceptual album. What is sung and who is singing share the same wound. The misfit, the victim, the star, the mannequin and the con artist all vie for the voice; yet none of them fully claim it as their own.

Rather than autonomous characters, they are transitional positions of a consciousness that shifts masks to narrate itself. “I wanted to kill my ‘self,’ my character,” he emphasizes. This approach also involves dismantling the signature as a guarantee of meaning: “In my first album, I introduced myself as Dillom. Here, it’s simply a voice speaking to you. It could be a voice in your head or different voices from different people.” By stepping away from the center, he explains, he opened himself up to speaking from a more shared experience, less tied to the tyranny of the ego. But fame imposes its own syntax: no matter what he does, his name will always headline the sentence.

The shift toward a self-referential narrative marks the album’s biggest conceptual change, while the true innovation lies in its approach to sound. The first auditory reference point was Charli xcx’s Brat (2024). A child of the “punkdemic,” and always tuned in to the mutations of the present, Dillom saw in those synthetic psalms a way of capturing an era hurtling at full speed toward itself. “I was really struck by everything [around] it — the movement, the marketing, the release, and the success,” he says. “Then I listened to the album, and I liked it. It’s not my favorite reco…
